chain.prompt: The camera does not move. Inside a speeding ambulance at night. The paramedic in the surgical mask twists from the heart monitor towards the cab and shouts forward, her gloved hand gripping the yellow grab rail as the whole compartment sways from side to side. The green trace on the monitor races. Behind her the second paramedic keeps pressing on the patient's chest. Blue light flickers through the windscreen. Filmed like real handheld news footage, quick movements blurring the way a film camera blurs them. One continuous shot, no cuts, no dialogue, no text. The camera does not move. Thanks.

chain.prompt: Using the provided image for everything (the angle, the light, the grain, the heart monitor, the paramedic at the yellow rail, the driver and the rainy windscreen), make the same photograph again with one thing corrected: the bag-valve mask over the old man's face is now squeezed by a second paramedic who is fully in the picture. He is a man in the same plain dark-green uniform, blue gloves and surgical mask, kneeling at the head end of the stretcher just behind the patient, leaning over him, both of his arms clearly connected to his shoulders as he squeezes the bag with one hand and holds the mask to the face with the other. Every hand in the frame belongs to a visible person. Vertical 9:16. Thanks.

The ambulance rolls slowly forward, so the bus shelter and its glowing poster slide gently across the side window while staying in view. Its blue emergency lights pulse across the wet door frame and the glass. Rain falls hard in the street-lamp glow and drops run down the window. The poster stays sharp and still. No talking. Siren and rain sounds only. Thanks.

chain.prompt: Vertical 9:16 photograph on 35 mm film at night, taken from inside the cab of a stopped ambulance, looking sideways out through its rain-spattered passenger window at a bus shelter on the pavement a few metres away. The dark edge of the window frame and the door's inner trim run down the left and bottom edges of the picture, lit in pulses of blue from the ambulance's own emergency lights bouncing off the wet bodywork, while raindrops and streaks cling to the outer corners of the glass. Through the clear middle of the window, filling well over half the frame's height and in sharp focus, is the shelter's backlit end-panel poster, glowing evenly from LED tubes behind it inside a thin dark metal frame: a glossy campaign portrait of the man from the reference image, head and shoulders, holding a phone to his right ear with his right hand, eyes to camera, a wide confident smile, on a flat deep magenta background, and beneath his face, in enormous heavy condensed white sans-serif capitals, the single line "SAVE OUR NHS". The shelter's glass side panes and perch bench sit dim and empty beside it; a sodium-orange street lamp behind the shelter hazes the rain into an orange glow, and the pavement in front reflects the poster's light in a long wet smear. Cold teal shadows, visible film grain, slight halation round the bright panel. The slogan is the only readable text in the frame: no party name, logo, small print, timetable writing, signs or number plates. Thanks.

A photorealistic vertical 9:16 photograph inside the back of a dark ministerial car at night in the rain, taken from low on the far end of the rear seat with a 28mm lens, so the cream leather seat and a folded-down armrest fill the bottom of the frame. On the armrest, sharp in the foreground, sits a small open glass jar of bright yellow lemon curd with a silver spoon in it and a crumpled napkin. Further back on the left, slumped into the seat, is an invented minister in his late fifties in a rumpled navy wool suit: a round, jowly face with pores and razor rash along the jaw, a small shaving nick on his chin, pink-rimmed tired eyes, wispy grey hair combed over, a crooked burgundy tie. He presses a phone to his ear, mouth shut in a tight, sulky line, nostrils flared, eyes rolled up at the roof lining. His head sits in the upper third of the frame, cut by the left edge. Through the rain-streaked window behind him, out of focus, an ambulance's blue lights pulse beside a red traffic light, throwing a cold blue band across one side of his face while a passing sodium street lamp lays an orange sweep over the other; the rest of the cabin sinks into teal-black, with a faint warm glow from a reading lamp in the roof. Shot on CineStill 800T, red halation round the lights outside, visible grain, underexposed, lifted blacks, handheld and slightly crooked. Thanks.

Vertical 9:16 cinematic night still from the cab of a UK ambulance, camera low between the two front seats, wide 24mm lens. Bottom of frame: the driver's hands strangling the steering wheel, knuckles pale, a sleeve of a plain dark-green uniform. The dashboard glows faintly. Top two-thirds: a windscreen streaming with rain, one wiper caught mid-sweep. Just beyond the bonnet, lit hard by the ambulance's headlights, a police motorcycle outrider in a soaked hi-vis jacket and white helmet stands astride his bike, one gloved hand held up flat, visor down, unmoved. Above him a red traffic light blooms through the wet glass, sodium-orange streetlamps smeared behind, blue emergency light flickering across the rain drops.
